sources.title: OpenChamber: Use it where you work; Quick start
sources.locator: Use it where you work; Quick start
sources.finding: OpenChamber has macOS, Windows and Linux desktop clients, a web/PWA client, VS Code extension and a CLI/server. Desktop bundles a matching OpenCode CLI; web/VS Code use an installed OpenCode CLI.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Install the app; PWA
sources.finding: Native iOS uses TestFlight beta and Android is a Canary APK. Phone apps can view sessions, reply and manage work; Safari/Chrome phone browsers can install the PWA. These clients connect to the user server.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Why OpenCode?
sources.finding: The core workspace uses OpenCode to run coding agents. Model/provider selection through OpenCode does not establish another named harness by itself.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Claude Code
sources.finding: The optional Claude Code integration uses the official Claude Agent SDK with the installed Claude Code CLI and supported sign-in. This is distinct from ordinary OpenCode provider configuration.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Claude Code
sources.finding: The Claude Code integration reuses Claude Pro or Max through the local Claude Code CLI sign-in without API keys. Setup can install the CLI and sign in.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Connect a provider; Where sign-ins live
sources.locator: Connect a provider; Where sign-ins live
sources.finding: OpenCode stores provider API keys and device-flow sign-ins. Custom OpenAI-compatible providers are configurable; signing into a model provider is separate from a native agent subscription.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Quick start
sources.finding: Desktop bundles OpenCode; CLI/Web requires Node.js 24.14+ and an installed OpenCode. Users start a local server protected with a UI password before connecting devices.

sources.title: OpenChamber: CLI for Web and PWA
sources.finding: Product CLI commands expose status, connect QR links, tunnels, startup control, logs, stop and update. A stable public session API was not inferred merely from the internal web app.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Add a server; Where it applies
sources.locator: Add a server; Where it applies
sources.finding: Users configure local command or remote URL MCP servers with headers/environment settings, scoped personally or per project. Servers can be disabled without deletion.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Extensions
sources.finding: Extensions can add git hosts, trackers, tools, UI and notification destinations. Local services require explicit permission in extension settings.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Start work from an issue or pull request
sources.locator: Start work from an issue or pull request
sources.finding: Git host issues and PRs become context for a new worktree/session; the message is not sent automatically. Supported hosts include GitHub, GitLab, Gitea, Forgejo and Gerrit changes.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Plans; Agents
sources.finding: Plans are editable Markdown files retained at project level, imported from text/Markdown and optionally moved into the repository. Agents update checklist steps, and the UI shows progress from the Steps section.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Agents
sources.finding: Agents can link todos to a plan and add dependencies on other todos in that plan. Ready-todo queries return unfinished items with completed prerequisites; standalone todos have no dependencies.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Notes; Memory
sources.finding: Project notes can be pinned into a session. Optional memory is off by default, scoped About you or Project, editable and forgettable, with agent-led tidy-up and visible changed markers.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Observations; Staying honest about staleness
sources.finding: Changes Walkthrough groups code-related edits, reads code/docs/tests and anchors its explanation to exact diff content; outdated or uncovered changes are labeled. This is explanation, not a code-quality verdict.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Project Notes, Todos and Plans; Todos
sources.locator: Project Notes, Todos and Plans; Todos
sources.finding: The native project todo checklist persists across sessions, supports checked completion and ordering, and can dispatch an item into current/new/worktree sessions. It is separate from external tracker items and the chat-session list.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Agents
sources.finding: The managed-server project knowledge tool lets agents read and edit the same notes, plans and todos humans see, link dependencies and query ready work. It is unavailable with an external OpenCode server or VS Code extension.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Multi-run
sources.finding: Multi-run starts several model sessions from one prompt, optionally each in its own worktree/branch. A failure to start one session does not prevent the rest from launching.

sources.title: OpenChamber: What you can ask
sources.finding: The native control tool creates sessions, sends prompts or follow-ups and can create worktree sessions. New-session prompts return immediately unless followed later.

sources.title: OpenChamber: What you can ask; Keep in mind
sources.locator: What you can ask; Keep in mind
sources.finding: An agent can create a child session with a selected model, list status, read the latest assistant response and send follow-ups. These tools belong to OpenChamber-managed OpenCode installations, not external servers or VS Code.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Create a task; Keep in mind
sources.locator: Create a task; Keep in mind
sources.finding: Native scheduled tasks send prompts in new sessions once, daily, weekly or by cron, optionally as goals. The OpenChamber server must stay running. Repository loop files require local enablement and renewed approval after material changes.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Stopping and resuming; Notifications
sources.finding: Stop and Pause abort the current turn and pause a goal; Resume re-arms it. Completion, blocking or exhausted budget emits one final notification while permission/questions/errors remain visible.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Sessions in Work
sources.finding: The In work sidebar groups ongoing sessions and worktrees, shows status and news, and permits marking work done or returning to it. No measured six-task navigation scenario was run.

sources.title: OpenChamber: What you can ask
sources.finding: Natural-language requests can create another model session, an isolated worktree or a schedule, and inspect results later. Project paths and arbitrary shell actions are outside this tool.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Keep in mind
sources.finding: The goal loop runs in the OpenChamber server, not the browser tab; closing the tab or locking the phone leaves the agent working, and the desktop app or openchamber process must stay running.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Worktree Sessions
sources.finding: A worktree session has its own checked-out copy of the repository on its own branch, keeping parallel sessions from editing the same files.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Clean up
sources.finding: Archived worktrees preserve sessions, uncommitted changes and branch data for restore, but ignored files such as node_modules and .env are not retained. Active sessions prevent archive removal.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Create one; Clean up
sources.finding: Project setup commands run after worktree creation and on restore; archived worktrees keep uncommitted changes and branches, but ignored files such as node_modules and .env are not kept, so setup commands must rebuild them.

sources.title: OpenChamber: How it works; Token budget
sources.finding: Goals have optional token budgets, an automatic-continuation cap and stop on turn errors. Blocking requires three consecutive stuck audits. Raising a budget and resuming is explicit.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Track work across projects
sources.finding: The UI shows working, waiting, finished and failed sessions with approvals, schedules, provider limits, token use and costs. These are documented statuses; reconnect consistency has not been tested.

sources.title: OpenChamber: What you see; Supported providers
sources.finding: Usage shows provider windows, model breakdown and pace; the agent usage tool can query those provider numbers and resets. This is provider allowance visibility, not a reconciled task invoice.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Allow ask deny; Three modes; Safety net
sources.locator: Allow ask deny; Three modes; Safety net
sources.finding: OpenCode permission rules allow, deny or ask. OpenChamber Ask every time, Safety net or Accept everything determines who answers ask; deny remains blocked. Safety net requires a classification provider and holds requests on uncertainty or timeout.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Agents
sources.finding: Agent-created notes are labeled and stale whole-document replacements can be refused against the prior text. This is not a tamper-resistant audit log.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Changes Walkthrough; Notes
sources.finding: A guided walkthrough groups related edits into ordered stops with code anchors, shows outdated/uncovered areas and supports line/file comments into chat. It is available on desktop, tablet and phone, excluding VS Code.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Inspect a running app; Guided changes walkthroughs
sources.locator: Inspect a running app; Guided changes walkthroughs
sources.finding: Preview places the running app beside chat and can send element screenshots, styles and errors as agent context. Diffs and guided walkthroughs retain review context. A cross-task artifact gallery was not established.

sources.title: OpenChamber: How it works
sources.finding: A separate model auditor compares the latest turn to the goal, continuing until done, blocked or budget/turn limits. It only sees the objective and latest reply, so this is not a general test/CI/spec approval gate.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Open and manage pull requests
sources.finding: The Git panel can create/update PRs, mark drafts ready and merge, with equivalent merge requests or Gerrit changes per host. Issues/PRs can start scoped worktree sessions.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Open and manage pull requests
sources.finding: Users create, update, mark ready and merge pull requests from the PR tab; GitLab offers merge and squash, and Gerrit Submit waits until the change meets its submit requirements. No production deployment authority was tested.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Staying honest about staleness
sources.finding: Walkthrough explanations are bound to exact code content. Changed anchors are marked Outdated and new uncovered changes are listed rather than silently reusing a verdict. This is not an approval-invalidating merge gate.

sources.title: OpenChamber: CLI for Web and PWA; Why OpenCode?
sources.locator: CLI for Web and PWA; Why OpenCode?
sources.finding: The full workspace/server can run on a user workstation or own server; optional Private Relay and tunnels provide connectivity rather than replacing the user runtime.

sources.title: OpenChamber: Enterprise mode
sources.finding: Enterprise mode restricts conversation-content features to configured OpenCode providers and can pin relay/classification endpoints and trusted extension repositories through an administrator policy file. This is a data-route policy, not evidence of SSO or a universal telemetry opt-out.

sources.title: OpenChamber: MIT License
sources.finding: The source application is available under a free-of-charge MIT grant. User model/provider usage and runtime hardware remain separate costs.

sources.title: OpenChamber: v2.7.0
sources.finding: OpenChamber v2.7.0 was published November 8. Mobile remains TestFlight/Canary access; public issues cover sidebar visibility, composer gestures and mobile shortcuts. Issue reports were not reproduced.

sources.title: OpenChamber: MIT License
sources.finding: The core application is free MIT software with user-hosted execution. Model and own-compute charges are excluded; mobile evaluation uses the documented beta/nightly channels.

sources.finding: The setting text says usage reports collect only app version, platform and runtime, with no personal data or code.

sources.title: OpenChamber Antigravity support at v2.7.0
sources.finding: OpenChamber v2.7.0 lists Antigravity as a quota provider reading OpenCode Antigravity account files. That does not establish an Antigravity coding-harness adapter.

sources.title: OpenChamber agent session adapter
sources.locator: createAgentSessionRuntime and OpenCode child sessions; integrations.mdx Claude Code
sources.finding: The scoped agent/session layer creates OpenCode sessions with provider/model selections. The separately documented Claude Code integration uses the official SDK/CLI. Bounded inspection of server startup, session/workflow adapters and integrations found no Codex, Cursor Agent, Gemini CLI, Pi, Grok, Aider or Antigravity coding-harness adapter. Quota/provider entries alone are not those harnesses.

sources.title: OpenChamber native browser and device authentication
sources.locator: UI auth controller; password/passkeys; client-auth remote clients and pairing
sources.finding: Native browser access uses a server password, passkeys and paired/trusted-device credentials under one shared server identity. Inspection of ui-auth and client-auth modules found no named human workspace/organization roles or SAML/OIDC enterprise SSO. Multiple paired devices do not establish distinct human shared prompting.

sources.title: OpenChamber managed runtime startup
sources.locator: Managed OpenCode process lifecycle; README CLI/server and Private Relay
sources.finding: The scoped server manages an installed/bundled OpenCode process on the workstation or user-operated server. Private Relay/tunnel access transports client traffic to that process rather than supplying vendor-operated execution.
